claim: Perceptual updating has been hypothesised to rely on a network reset modulated by bursts of ascending neuromodulatory neurotransmitters, such as noradrenaline, abruptly altering the brain's susceptibility to changing sensory activity.
source: Perceptual updating has been hypothesised to rely on a network reset modulated by bursts of ascending neuromodulatory neurotransmitters, such as noradrenaline, abruptly altering the brain's susceptibility to changing sensory activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis statement that frames the research question, drawing on established theoretical frameworks about neuromodulation.

claim: Qualitative shifts in the perceptual interpretation of an ambiguous image were associated with peaks in pupil diameter.
source: Behaviourally, qualitative shifts in the perceptual interpretation of an ambiguous image were associated with peaks in pupil diameter, an indirect readout of phasic bursts in neuromodulatory tone.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the pupillometry experiment showing temporal correlation between perceptual switches and pupil diameter changes.

claim: Pupil diameter is an indirect readout of phasic bursts in neuromodulatory tone.
source: Behaviourally, qualitative shifts in the perceptual interpretation of an ambiguous image were associated with peaks in pupil diameter, an indirect readout of phasic bursts in neuromodulatory tone.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the relationship between pupil diameter and neuromodulatory activity.

claim: Stimulus ambiguity drives neuromodulatory tone, leading to heightened neural gain, hastening perceptual switches.
source: We further hypothesised that stimulus ambiguity drives neuromodulatory tone, leading to heightened neural gain, hastening perceptual switches.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested through computational modeling and empirical data.

claim: Higher gain accelerated perceptual switching by transiently destabilising the network's dynamical regime in periods of maximal uncertainty.
source: As predicted, higher gain accelerated perceptual switching by transiently destabilising the network's dynamical regime in periods of maximal uncertainty.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results from the RNN experiments.

claim: Perceptual switches occur with peaks in low-dimensional brain state velocity.
source: We leveraged a low-dimensional readout of the RNN dynamics to develop two novel macroscale predictions: perceptual switches should occur with peaks in low-dimensional brain state velocity and with a flattened egocentric energy landscape.
evidence: This prediction was derived from RNN modeling and confirmed in fMRI data.

claim: Perceptual switches occur with a flattened egocentric energy landscape.
source: We leveraged a low-dimensional readout of the RNN dynamics to develop two novel macroscale predictions: perceptual switches should occur with peaks in low-dimensional brain state velocity and with a flattened egocentric energy landscape.
evidence: This prediction was derived from RNN modeling and confirmed in fMRI data.

claim: The identity of sensory inputs is inherently ambiguous because the overwhelming majority of neurons in our brains have only indirect interactions with the external world.
source: The overwhelming majority of neurons in our brains have only indirect interactions with the external world. This means that the identity of sensory inputs is inherently ambiguous (Bogacz, 2017; Flounders et al., 2019; Friston, 2005; Hohwy, 2013; Clark, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work in neuroscience and perception.

claim: The equivocal nature of perceptual input is overcome by incorporating prior information about the causal structure of the world into sensory inferences.
source: The equivocal nature of perceptual input is overcome by incorporating prior information about the causal structure of the world into sensory inferences.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on predictive coding and Bayesian brain frameworks.

claim: In ambiguous scenarios, observers periodically switch between mutually exclusive percepts.
source: This is clearly evidenced in laboratory experiments that present participants with sensory inputs that offer two equally valid yet mutually exclusive perceptual interpretations (e.g. the Necker cube illusion and binocular rivalry): in these ambiguous scenarios, observers periodically switch between mutually exclusive percepts (Hohwy et al., 2008; Alais and Blake, 2005; van Ee, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies on bistable perception.

claim: Perceptual awareness is remarkably stable outside of conditions of extreme perceptual ambiguity.
source: Outside of conditions of extreme perceptual ambiguity, perceptual awareness is remarkably stable, suggesting that the nervous system can rapidly (and flexibly) identify the best 'match' between visual data and a stable (likely known) stimulus category (Hohwy et al., 2008; Hohwy, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work on perceptual stability.

claim: Adaptive behaviour requires that the relative reliability of prior information and current sensory input are made suitably contextually dependent.
source: Importantly, this process of combining ambiguous sensory input with prior information must be dynamic: adaptive behaviour requires that the relative reliability of prior information and current sensory input are made suitably contextually dependent (Moran et al., 2013; Shine et al., 2021; Parr and Friston, 2018; Parr and Friston, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on adaptive inference and predictive coding.

claim: Neuroimaging studies investigating perceptual updating and switches have typically identified a distributed set of regions within the cerebral cortex.
source: Neuroimaging studies investigating perceptual updating and switches have typically identified a distributed set of regions within the cerebral cortex (Stöttinger et al., 2015; Weilnhammer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Cortical regions are presumed to play a role in attentional shifts driving switches in perceptual contents by selectively boosting activity within the relevant circuits.
source: These cortical regions are presumed to play a role in attentional shifts driving switches in perceptual contents by selectively boosting activity within the relevant circuits (Weilnhammer et al., 2017; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Desimone and Duncan, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on attention and neural gain.

claim: Attention plays a prominent role in determining the contents of perception in bistable perception tasks where competition is not resolved at low-levels of the visual hierarchy.
source: This interpretation is complemented by behavioural evidence showing that attention plays a prominent role in determining the contents of perception in bistable perception tasks where competition is not resolved at low-levels of the visual hierarchy (Meng and Tong, 2004; Dieter and Tadin, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies on attention and bistable perception.

claim: Computational models of perceptual decision-making typically consist of winner-take-all competition between cortical populations.
source: Similarly, computational models of perceptual decision-making typically consist of winner-take-all competition between cortical populations (Wong and Wang, 2006; Eckhoff et al., 2011; Wang, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: The ability to flexibly respond to ambiguous visual inputs according to changing task demands is present across phylogeny.
source: Yet, the ability to flexibly respond to ambiguous visual inputs according to changing task demands is a feature that is present across phylogeny (Cisek, 2019) and hence is present in a wide variety of animals that have poorly developed cerebral cortices (Carter et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative neuroscience studies.

claim: Phasic change in the ascending arousal system have been linked to moment-by-moment adaptive updates in the relative weighting of prior information, sensory input, and the urgency of the perceptual decision process through neuromodulatory-mediated alterations in neural gain.
source: Indeed, phasic change in the highly conserved ascending arousal system have been linked to moment-by-moment adaptive updates in the relative weighting of prior information, sensory input, and the urgency of the perceptual decision process through neuromodulatory-mediated alterations in neural gain (Sales et al., 2019; Vincent et al., 2019; Jordan and Keller, 2023; Murphy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on neuromodulation and decision-making.

claim: The ascending neuromodulatory system, and specifically the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC), is well-suited to modulate the large-scale, brain state switches required to flexibly alter perceptual contents.
source: The ascending neuromodulatory system, and specifically the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC), is well-suited to modulate the large-scale, brain state switches required to flexibly alter perceptual contents (Szabadi, 2018; Briand et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroanatomical and neurophysiological studies.

claim: The LC sends projections throughout the central nervous system, wherein its axons release noradrenaline, which in turn modulate the excitability of targeted regions.
source: While the cell body of the LC is located in the brainstem, the nucleus sends projections throughout the central nervous system, wherein its axons release noradrenaline, which in turn modulate the excitability of targeted regions (Shine et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroanatomical studies.

claim: The phasic release of noradrenaline from the LC acts as a 'network reset' signal, which effectively disrupts ongoing processing, and allows animals to reconfigure their ongoing neural dynamics towards more salient processes.
source: In previous work, it has been argued that the phasic release of noradrenaline from the LC acts as a 'network reset' signal, which effectively disrupts ongoing processing, and hence allows animals to reconfigure their ongoing neural dynamics towards more salient (and hopefully, behaviourally relevant) processes (Sara, 2009; Jacob and Nienborg, 2018; Bouret and Sara, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work on LC function.

claim: When a stimulus is task-relevant, pupil diameter is tightly linked to switches in the content of perception.
source: Preliminary evidence in the context of bistable perception has shown that when a stimulus is task-relevant, pupil diameter (a non-specific and indirect readout of phasic LC activity [Joshi and Gold, 2020; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008; Pfeffer et al., 2022; de Gee et al., 2020] and neuromodulatory tone) is tightly linked to switches in the content of perception (Murphy et al., 2014; Einhäuser et al., 2008; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on pupillometry and bistable perception.

claim: Linking perceptual updates to fluctuations in neuromodulatory tone recapitulates the phasic-tonic firing rate pattern known to characterise LC spiking dynamics and improves performance in reinforcement learning tasks.
source: In line with this, recent modelling has shown that linking perceptual updates to fluctuations in neuromodulatory tone recapitulates the phasic-tonic firing rate pattern known to characterise LC spiking dynamics and improves performance in reinforcement learning tasks (Sales et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claim: Task-related perceptual switches can be modulated by phasic bursts of LC activity, which act as a 'network reset', flattening the whole-brain energy landscape and allowing cortical dynamics to evolve into a new state thereby changing the contents of perception.
source: Based on previous work (Sara, 2009; Jacob and Nienborg, 2018; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Shine, 2019; Wainstein et al., 2021), and the projections of the LC to many of the regions implicated in whole-brain imaging studies of perceptual uncertainty (Samuels and Szabadi, 2008; de Gee et al., 2014; de Gee et al., 2017), we hypothesised that task-related perceptual switches can be modulated by phasic bursts of LC activity, which act as a 'network reset' (Bouret and Sara, 2005), flattening the whole-brain energy landscape (Munn et al., 2021) and thus allowing cortical dynamics to evolve into a new state thereby changing the contents of perception.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by citations to previous work and tested through experiments.

claim: Pupil diameter peaked at the point of the perceptual switch and predicted their timing.
source: We observed that pupil diameter peaked at the point of the perceptual switch and predicted their timing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the pupillometry experiment.

claim: An increase in the phasic pupillary response was observed approximately three trials before participants switched to a new perceptual category.
source: We observed a clear increase in the phasic pupillary response approximately three trials before participants switched to a new perceptual category, potentially reflecting the onset of increased ambiguity towards a new object (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The pupillary response peaked at the point of the perceptual switch, corresponding to the maximum pupil diameter.
source: This response peaked at the point of the perceptual switch, corresponding to the maximum pupil diameter (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the mean pupil response starting three images before the change point (mean β=0.22; t(32) = 8.02, p=2.3 × 10−19), before returning to baseline levels.
source: Further analysis revealed a significant increase in the mean pupil response starting three images before the change point (mean β=0.22; t(32) = 8.02, p=2.3 × 10−19), before returning to baseline levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pupillometry data.

claim: An inverse relationship was observed between evoked pupil diameter and the trial marking the perceptual switch (mean β=–0.19, t(27)=–2.6452, p=6.7 × 10⁻³, SD=0.3880).
source: As expected, we observed an inverse relationship between evoked pupil diameter and the trial marking the perceptual switch (mean β=–0.19, t(27)=–2.6452, p=6.7 × 10⁻³, SD=0.3880).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pupillometry data.

claim: Earlier responses showed a positive relationship with higher evoked pupil diameter during the switch epoch.
source: Earlier responses showed a positive relationship with higher evoked pupil diameter during the switch epoch (Figure 1D, red), whereas later responses were associated with a more constricted pupil (Figure 1D, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Noradrenaline alters neural gain.
source: Along with others (Kosciessa et al., 2021; Eldar et al., 2013; Urai et al., 2017; Kloosterman et al., 2015), we have used a combination of computational modelling (Shine et al., 2018; Müller et al., 2020), neurobiological theory (Shine et al., 2021), and multi-model neuroimaging (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Carter et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2014; Szabadi, 2018) to suggest that noradrenaline alters neural gain (Servan-schreiber, 2016; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005), which in turn affects inter-regional communication flattening the energy landscape traversed by the brain's dynamics allowing the brain state to jump between perceptual attractors more easily.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational, theoretical, and neuroimaging studies.

claim: All networks achieved near-perfect behavioural accuracy (0.97±0.02) following training.
source: Following training, all networks achieved near-perfect behavioural accuracy (0.97±0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the RNN training.

claim: 80.58±6.34% of the variance in RNN activity was explained by the first principal component (PC1).
source: The set of PCs was low-dimensional, with 80.58±6.34% of the variance explained by the first principal component (PC1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNN data.

claim: Increased gain leads to earlier 'perceptual switches' in the network output whereas low gain caused later switches.
source: As predicted, increased gain (red; corresponding to heightened adrenergic tone) leads to earlier 'perceptual switches' in the network output whereas low gain caused later switches (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNN modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The networks had learned to complete the task by segregating both excitatory and inhibitory units into two stimulus-selective clusters.
source: Inspection of the firing rates sorted by input weights revealed that the networks had learned to complete the task by segregating both excitatory and inhibitory units into two stimulus-selective clusters (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNN firing rates shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lesioning the inhibitory units strongly selective for the initially dominant population greatly slowed perceptual switches.
source: In line with our prediction, lesioning the inhibitory units strongly selective for the initially dominant population greatly slowed perceptual switches (Figure 2F, upper), whereas lesioning the population selective for the stimulus the input morphs into removed the speeding effect of gain but had a comparatively small slowing effect on perceptual switches (Figure 2F, lower).
evidence: This claim is supported by lesion analysis of the RNN shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Heightened gain at points of ambiguity accelerates perceptual switches by transiently pushing the dynamics into an unstable regime.
source: At the population level, therefore, heightened gain at points of ambiguity accelerates perceptual switches by transiently pushing the dynamics into an unstable regime.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNN dynamical analysis.

claim: The unstable regime replaces the fixed-point attractor representing the input with an oscillatory regime that actively inhibits the currently dominant population and boosts the competing population.
source: This regime replaces the fixed-point attractor representing the input with an oscillatory regime that actively inhibits the currently dominant population and boosts the competing population, before transitioning back to a stable (approximate) fixed-point attractor representing the new stimulus (Figure 3F–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNN dynamical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Peaks in BOLD within the LC precede large changes in brain state dynamics.
source: In recent work (Munn et al., 2021, Taylor et al., 2022), we have shown that peaks in BOLD within the LC precede large changes in brain state dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work from the authors.

claim: The resultant low-dimensional trajectories all showed a change in direction around the timepoint of the switch in network output from category 1 to category 2.
source: The resultant low-dimensional trajectories all showed a change in direction around the timepoint of the switch in network output from category 1 to category 2 (and v.v.; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNN trajectories shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A small number of PCs mapped onto distributed regions across the brain and explained a substantial proportion of the variance observed in the task (PC1-3 explained 32% of the total variance).
source: Consistent with previous work (Shine et al., 2019), a small number of PCs mapped onto distributed regions across the brain (Figure 5A) and explained a substantial proportion of the variance observed in the task (PC1-3 explained 32% of the total variance).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both PC2 and PC3 showed a pronounced, isolated peak around the switch point across trials.
source: PC1 was not selectively aligned with switches, both PC2 and PC3 showed a pronounced, isolated peak around the switch point across trials (Figure 5B), with PC2 showing the most robust task-related engagement (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by principal component regression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The engagement of both PC2 and PC3 during the switch point was greater than to be expected by chance.
source: The dotted grey line in Figure 5B denotes the 95th percentile of the null distribution, and clearly shows that the engagement of both PC2 and PC3 during the switch point was greater than to be expected by chance.
evidence: This claim is supported by permutation testing shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A regression with PC2 and PC3 as predictors and the evoked activity derived from the original BOLD time series as the dependent variable resulted in variance accounted for of 88% (R2=0.88, β=0.99, p=9.2 × 10–178).
source: Furthermore, to validate that the perceptual switch was predominantly represented by PC2 and PC3 (Figure 5D), we conducted a regression with these two PCs as predictors and the evoked activity derived from the original BOLD time series as the dependent variable. The resulting variance accounted for was 88% (R2=0.88, β=0.99, p=9.2 × 10–178).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis of fMRI data.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the map for 'switching' and both PC2 (r=0.453, p=3.041 × 10–18) and PC3 (r=0.115, p=0.037).
source: We observed a significant positive correlation between the map for 'switching' and both PC2 (r=0.453, p=3.041 × 10–18) and PC3 (r=0.115, p=0.037); however, the correlation for PC3 was much lower than PC3, suggesting that PC2 was a better match for 'switching'.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis with neurosynth maps.

claim: A partial correlation analysis revealed that PC2 was selectively associated with 'switching' and 'attention'.
source: The spatial map of PC2 was also positively correlated with other terms putatively associated with the ambiguous figures task (notably, 'effort', 'load', and 'attention'; all r>0.2; and not with 'episodic', which was included as a negative control), a partial correlation analysis revealed that PC2 was selectively associated with 'switching' and 'attention' (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A hierarchical modular decomposition approach revealed three main clusters in the time-averaged functional connectivity matrix.
source: To test this hypothesis, we clustered the time-averaged functional connectivity matrix using a hierarchical modular decomposition approach (see 'Methods') – doing so revealed three main clusters (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A robust correlation was observed between a joint histogram of integration and segregation measures with the sum of subject-specific regression coefficients for PC2 and PC3 (p<0.05 following permutation testing).
source: We then correlated a joint histogram of these measures with the sum of subject-specific regression coefficients for PC2 and PC3 and observed a robust correlation with integration (Figure 5F; p<0.05 following permutation testing).
evidence: This claim is supported by network topology analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PC2 was maximally displaced at the perceptual change, suggesting that the brain state showed a substantial shift from baseline during the perceptual change.
source: Using this approach, we observed that PC2 was maximally displaced at the perceptual change, suggesting that the brain state showed a substantial shift from baseline during the perceptual change.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PC2 displacement in fMRI data.

claim: Energy showed a U-shaped pattern around the perceptual change point – that is, with a minimum value in the perceptual change along with the first and last images.
source: Energy (log[1/pswitch]; see 'Methods') showed a U-shaped pattern around the perceptual change point – that is, with a minimum value in the perceptual change along with the first and last images (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by energy landscape analysis shown in Figures 6B-D.

claim: The brain state reduced the amount of energy per displacement towards its minimum around the perceptual change.
source: As predicted, the brain state reduced the amount of energy per displacement towards its minimum around the perceptual change (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by energy landscape analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PC2 showed a peak in velocity at the change point.
source: As predicted (Figure 6C), we found evidence that PC2 showed a peak in velocity at the change point (Figure 6D) providing confirmatory evidence that the low-dimensional brain state dynamics observed in whole-brain fMRI were highly similar to those observed in the trained RNN.
evidence: This claim is supported by velocity analysis of PC2 shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The ascending arousal system is involved in the modulation of dynamic brain state topography during task-relevant perceptual switches.
source: Here, we studied the relationship between the ascending arousal system, low-dimensional neuronal trajectories and energy landscape dynamics during a perceptual switch task. Our results provide evidence that the ascending arousal system is involved in the modulation of dynamic brain state topography during task-relevant perceptual switches.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined evidence from pupillometry, RNN modeling, and fMRI experiments.

claim: The ascending arousal system facilitates state changes in the content of perception by transiently increasing neural gain.
source: Together, these results suggest that the ascending arousal system facilitates state changes in the content of perception by transiently increasing neural gain – acting in a manner analogous to an external forcing function transiently increasing kinetic energy in the system – flattening the ego-centric energy landscape and thereby reducing the energy needed to reset the system topography in an adaptive and task-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined evidence from all experiments.

claim: The relationship between perception and pupil diameter found here is consistent with the role of the ascending neuromodulation in cognition and attention.
source: The relationship between perception and pupil diameter found here is consistent with the role of the ascending neuromodulation in cognition and attention (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Wainstein et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's findings and citations to previous work.

claim: The LC dynamically changes its activity according to external and cognitive demands imposed on the system.
source: For instance, the LC dynamically changes its activity according to external and cognitive demands imposed on the system (Joshi et al., 2016; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Wainstein et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2017; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on LC function.

claim: The widespread excitatory projections of the noradrenergic arousal system mediate the systems-level reconfigurations of cortical network architecture via uncertainty-driven alterations in neural gain.
source: Specifically, we suggest that the widespread excitatory projections of the noradrenergic arousal system mediate the systems-level reconfigurations of cortical network architecture (Totah et al., 2019; Zerbi et al., 2019) via uncertainty-driven alterations in neural gain.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the study's findings and citations to previous work.

claim: More highly conserved features of the nervous system may play a role in driving task-relevant switches in the contents of perception.
source: This suggests that more highly conserved features of the nervous system may play a role in driving task-relevant switches in the contents of perception.
evidence: This is a concluding inference based on the study's findings.

claim: 35 subjects performed a perceptual decision-making perceptual task while pupil diameter was recorded.
source: There were two independent groups analysed in this study: 35 subjects performed a perceptual decision-making perceptual task while pupil diameter was recorded; and a separate group of 17 subjects performed a version of the task adapted for the MRI scanner.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the study design.

claim: A separate group of 17 subjects performed a version of the task adapted for the MRI scanner.
source: There were two independent groups analysed in this study: 35 subjects performed a perceptual decision-making perceptual task while pupil diameter was recorded; and a separate group of 17 subjects performed a version of the task adapted for the MRI scanner.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the study design.

claim: The task consisted of a set of continuously transforming images that transition from an initial object into a second object, while preserving basic psychophysical attributes.
source: Briefly, the task consisted of a set of continuously transforming images that transition from an initial object (e.g. a shark) into a second object (e.g. a plane), while preserving basic psychophysical attributes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental task.

claim: Even though the task stimuli change incrementally and linearly, with maximal ambiguity at the mid-point of each trial, awareness of a change in the stimulus is known to 'pop out', often at different times on each trial.
source: Crucially, even though the task stimuli change incrementally and linearly, with maximal ambiguity at the mid-point of each trial (the peak of the dotted line curve in Figure 1A), awareness of a change in the stimulus is known to 'pop out', often at different times on each trial (Stöttinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and the task design.

claim: Participants viewed 20 unique sets of images, each of which morphed from a starting image into a second image through 15 equally spaced intermittent stages.
source: Participants viewed 20 unique sets of images, each of which morphed from a starting image into a second image through 15 equally spaced intermittent stages (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental task.

claim: The linear nature of the morphing procedure meant that luminance levels were kept constant across all trials.
source: The linear nature of the morphing procedure meant that luminance levels (which could otherwise bias pupil diameter; Szabadi, 2018; Joshi and Gold, 2020; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008) were kept constant across all trials.
evidence: This is a methodological description explaining a control for potential confounds.

claim: Motor preparation was controlled by requiring subjects to press a button on each image.
source: Additionally, motor preparation was controlled by requiring subjects to press a button on each image (indicating the content of their perception).
evidence: This is a methodological description explaining a control for potential confounds.

claim: 50 continuous time RNNs were trained constrained to respect Dale's law.
source: To test whether our hypothesised neuromodulatory mechanism could recapitulate the behaviour we observed in the ambiguous figures task, we trained 50 continuous time RNNs constrained to respect Dale's law (i.e. 80/20 split of purely excitatory/inhibitory units; Song et al., 2016; Yang and Wang, 2020) to perform a perceptual change detection task analogous to the task performed by our participants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the computational modeling approach.

claim: The input and readout weights were constrained to be purely excitatory and only the firing rate of excitatory units contributed to the readout.
source: The input and readout weights were constrained to be purely excitatory and only the firing rate of excitatory units contributed to the readout (Song et al., 2016; see 'Methods').
evidence: This is a methodological description of the RNN architecture.

claim: A total of 17 (six males) neurologically healthy participants with normal or corrected to normal vision took part in the fMRI study (mean age 27.65±8.01).
source: A total of 17 (six males) neurologically healthy participants with normal or corrected to normal vision took part in the fMRI study (mean age 27.65±8.01).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the participant sample.

claim: A separate cohort of 35 participants performed the task while simultaneous pupil diameter was recorded using an eye tracker device.
source: A separate cohort of 35 participants performed the task while simultaneous pupil diameter was recorded using an eye tracker device (SR Research, 1000 Hz).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the participant sample and data collection.
